utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours, IT-95-16-T. The Prosector versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. We resume with the examination-in-chief of Mr. Grebenar. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning. We stopped yesterday with the order or report that you got from the guards and why you went to visit Ms. Marin Papic to see what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that you called Mario Cerkez and then after some time he called you back and you received information to remain on watch?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't speak to Mario, I spoke to the person on duty at the command office. Mario called me back later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do after that, after you received this information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: After talking to Mario and his advice to continue with our watch, that there were some reports that even he wasn't sure about on how truthful or reliable they were, so to continue with our watch. Then with the two men who woke me up, I agreed with them for one of them to go towards the upper part of the village, one to tour the central part of the village, and then I went to the lower part of the village to see if the men who were on watch were still there, and to make sure that they remained there, because the guard was supposed to stay there until 5.00. So the watch would stop at 5.00. We agreed to look for these men and to stay with them for some time to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your watches went on until 5.00 a.m.; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, they were from 9.00 in the evening 'til 5.00 a.m. It was some kind of internal agreement. The Muslim watches too went on from 9.00 in the evening 'til 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen in the village at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Nothing unusual. I went towards the lower part of the village and when I got there to look for the men who were on watch, I didn't find them on the road or around the houses, but at that time you could already hear shooting from the direction of Vitez, from Mahala. So you could hear shooting already at that time. So I went into the house of one of the men and I found the other two men who were supposed to be on watch. They had finished their shift. They were drinking coffee. So there was no point in them going to bed any more. So they just sat down to have some coffee. I told them, well, there is shooting coming from the direction of Vitez and Ahmici, we would really need to go out to see what was going on. So that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you evacuate the civilians at that time? Did you tell them to go to shelters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: No. At that time, no. We felt there was still no need to do that. We weren't aware of what was going to happen or whether anything was going to happen. The civilians were still asleep. I didn't even go to my house to see my wife, my children, my mother, my father. They were all sleeping at the house. It was only around 7.00 or 8.00 people started to get up. The detonations, the shooting became louder, and then it became obvious that something really serious was happening. So as people started to wake up, they started to go to cellars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the shooting begin in the village, and from what side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: The shooting in the village -- well, the shelling started first. The shelling in the lower part of the village around my house, and then underneath, below my house. There was also a warehouse of construction material there, so this seemed to be a good orientation point because all the Croatian houses were around that warehouse. So the shells started to fall sometime before 9.00 a.m., around 9.00 a.m. a couple of shells dropped. And then shortly after that you could hear artillery from the direction of Vrhovine and Prnjavor. It was sporadic, nothing --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So which weapons, what kind of firing was this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: In the beginning there were shells and then infantry weapons. I'm not a military expert, it's hard to tell, but as time went on I could notice that these were some more powerful weapons because then they started to hit us from Sljivcica, Tolovici, Vjetrenica, Vrhovine, I don't think this could have been done with just regular automatic rifles. It had to have been a range of at least 1.000 or 1.500 metres. So I assumed there were more powerful weapons such as brownings or machine guns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The shelling, which direction did the shells come from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Well, to us, it seemed that they came from every direction. When the shelling began, depending on where everywhere was, and since we didn't have any kind of organised defence, we had no trenches, no defence line in the village. It was impossible to structure that. So simply people would come out of their houses and they would take some kind of defensive position. I tried from the lower part of the village to the central part, all the way to the upper part of the village at around 9.00, 9.30, I tried to go and tour all of the positions to see what was going on, whether there were any wounded people, because the grenades were falling. I heard that there was one person that was wounded, but it turned out to be just a scratch on his neck. It was a young man, so we bandaged him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please show us on the map where the shelling came from. You mentioned Sljivcica, Vrhovine, Vjetrenica, Tolovici.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't respond fully where the shells came from. I just wanted to say that when I went from one group to another, so in the lower part of the village they were saying we are getting shelled on from Sljivcica. When I got to the centre of the village they said the grenades are coming from Vrhovine. The upper part of the village was saying that the shells were coming from Preocica and Tolovici. So it was very hard at that time to determine where the shells came from. But they had grenade launchers also from the direction of Tolovici where the Muslims were after the Serbs left. I can show you this on the map. Will you be able to hear me? So Poculica is here. So from here from the direction of Tolovici, the direction of Vrhovine, and then in that part. So towards Barin Gaj, since this is an inhabited area, this is where the forest is, and the mortars were probably from the forest and from the lower part of the village. Then from Vjetrenica, but I can't see it here on the map, Preocica should be somewhere around here. Then Tolovici is right here from the lower part of the -- of Tolovici, as far as we could tell. Sljivcica, it's not very easy to see, but it's there. It's close to Sivrino Selo. That's where Sljivcica should be. There's a kind of elevation there, a hill, and it's an elevation, a dominant point as compared to the village. So this is where the mortar shelling came from and machine gun fire. I'm not sure whether it could have been mortar shelling from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the shelling start also from the back besides the shelling that you are describing now? Was there any shooting in the village between the upper and the lower part of the village, perhaps, or did this not happen at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: At that time, so this was probably some time between 9.00 and 9.30 in the morning, there was no direct fighting in the village itself. It all came at a distance. They were shelling us from a distance. And then at around 9.30 in the central part of the village, where we -- there was one Muslim house there, two or three Croatian, and then a Muslim. So this was the mixed part of the village. Then the son of Hasim Krehic, I think his name was Hamid or Ahmed, I'm not sure about his first name. At about 9.30 he came with an automatic machine gun and he went towards the upper part of the village, towards the mosque. And since the Croats were there in front of their houses with guns also, there were neighbours, so there were old Croatian houses around this house. I asked him, "Where are you going?" And he said, "I am afraid I don't know what's going on, so I am going up there to see what's happening." In the meantime, going around the village with another two men, I came by that place and he said he was going to the upper part of the village to shoot. And I said, "Well, it wouldn't be good for you to go up there with that rifle, because you could fire at us from there. There is no problem, you can leave your rifle and then go up there and see what's going on, and see if there is anybody there that we could talk to, because this is something that seems to be serious, and I don't think that things will turn out well." He did seem afraid, and he thought about it for a little while. He was standing there with his rifle. He was afraid to go there and he was afraid to stay. So this is what I could tell. This was a young man, he was maybe 18, and I knew him. So he trusted us. But he was afraid, simply afraid. In the meantime, Abaz Causevic came by and asked us what's going on. "They are saying up there that the army has arrived and the Mujahedins are taking your people to Prnjavor, and they told everybody that they will kill one person every five minutes unless Hasim gets up there, because they received information up there that we had killed Hasim's son, so they wanted to take revenge." And I said, but Abaz, you can see that this young man is here and he has a rifle and we are just discussing what the best thing is to do. We talked. "He can go, he can leave the rifle here, but we don't want to let him go up there if he is going to shoot against us. So he can go, he can leave the rifle, he can leave the rifle at his house, go there with you, Abaz, and see if you can do something." Then I also asked Abaz, "Well, is this really war, what's the situation up there?" And he just waved his hand and he said, "Well, I am in a hurry now. I want to take him up there and I'll come back later and we'll try to do something." Abaz would participate in our talks before. He was a person whom it was possible to talk to. So that's what happened, the two of them went up there together. Then after half an hour, I don't know the military expressions, but I think a frontal attack, I think that's what it's called, started from the area of the mosque, also the infantry from the direction of Vjeternice, Preocica. They came, they were approaching, they were capturing our houses, and you could hear stronger firing. So I found out about all of this because my neighbours, my Croatian neighbours, who were there around there houses had escaped, and they came to the lower part of the village. This is what they told me. They said it was chaos up there, it was full of the army. They were shooting. So they simply fled to the lower part of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us, at the time the attacks started from the upper part of the village, did you see Muslim civilians in the houses?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: When Ahmid went to the upper part of the village, after that I went up there up to maybe just below the mosque, and that's where my people were around their houses. So coming back from there I saw a man called Pektas, he was in front of his home with his wife. I said, "Well, neighbour, what's happening?" And then later, at about 11.30, when Anto Jurecevic was wounded above the mosque, he was a civilian, he was going to his barn to feed his cattle, so he was wounded while he was coming out of the barn. So some people brought him to the central part of the village. We took him. And the shooting was much, much stronger at that time. It was going on in between the houses. And that's where I saw Pektas and his wife. They had been in the cellar. And when we came by, they came out and they were asking, "Neighbour, what's happening? Is this possible?" They were asking about Anto, how is he, was he seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you manage to get in contact with anybody regarding the wounded person? Were the telephone lines operating?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes. I managed to get in touch with the headquarters. I had the number of the headquarters, but it was very difficult to get through because it was busy all the time. I think this was the communication centre. So I had some kind of -- I had a number of one of the people on duty there, and I said that there was chaos in Poculica. I had a wounded person and would somebody tell me what to do, what was going on. We simply weren't prepared for any of that. We didn't know what to do. So then they said that they would try to send an ambulance or some kind of vehicle. And this is what happened, I think sometime before 11.30. Even though already at that time in Dubravica on the road, the Muslim army was there near Sivrino Selo, because when the driver came he said they -- I had problems getting through, and I told them there was a wounded person in question. But I don't know whether they were going to let me go back. So he couldn't get all the way to the upper part of the village in his vehicle, because he had to leave it in the lower part, because there was a lot of shooting already. So then we took the wounded person in between the houses to the lower part of the village. We put him in the ambulance and he was transported to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you could see the Muslim army near Dubravica, what did the driver of the ambulance tell you? Was this towards the road, in the direction of the road? Could you please indicate to us where Dubravica is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Here, on this map, Dubravica is here (indicating) but we call that lower Dubravica because that's a separate road which leads to Tolovici, but there is upper Dubravica as well, and that is this road which goes straight to Poculica. So all the inhabited places are here, as far as I can see, so this is the Dubravica that I'm talking about, upper Dubravica, and then Sivrino Selo is there and then Sljivcica, and they were right here. They came up to this part of Dubravica, upper Dubravica, and the other place is called Donja Dubravica, lower Dubravica, or Krizancevo Selo. So this is a different road that goes through Donja Dubravica to Krizancevo Selo towards Tolovici, so this is a dead-end road. And then this is the other road that goes straight to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us if you saw the army in the village? Did you see soldiers? What kind of insignia did they have or did you just shoot blindly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: I wasn't shooting at that time, and I didn't see anybody to shoot at then. In the lower part of the village, the only thing that we could shoot in -- I mean, we didn't really see. They were shooting from quite a distance, so we didn't have strong weapons to shoot as far as Sljivcica, and you couldn't see anybody. But the people in the upper part of the village had close encounters. The people who escaped had said that they had seen the Mujahedin and people they hadn't seen until that time. They had various uniforms, camouflage uniforms, black uniforms, and there were even some who had scarves wrapped around their heads, and according to what they said, and they were afraid so they could have exaggerated, but from the talks we had with them, they said there were at least three or four different kinds of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at 12.00?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: In around 12.00, I was again in the lower part of the village, and I was going around visiting all the civilians. I was trying to encourage them. I don't even remember what exactly we were doing. We weren't quite sure what to do. We weren't doing anything radical. Before that, at around 11.30 when I was in the central part of the village, Krehic Asim, the young man had come back, the one who had gone up there. I was maybe a couple of houses below, and then somebody came and said, "Krehic is looking for you," Hamed or Ahmed, I'm not sure of the name. She said, "He's come back and he's asking about you. He's looking for you," and this other guy who is with me, Jura, I think. So we went up there together, and I asked him, "What's going on?" This young man was really scared. There were tears in his eyes. He said, "Dragan, I really don't know what's going on, but it's full of the army and the Mujahedin up there. The army has arrived from Zenica. They're taking your people to Prnjavor. They've been captured, and they're preparing to take the village, to kill everybody, to burn it." His voice was shaking, and I said, "Well, is there anyone there that we could talk to? What did you tell them?" And he said, "No, there's nobody there. Nobody amongst us is being asked anything." Then I asked him, "Why did you come to see me? What did you want? What can you tell me? What can you convey to me?" And he said, "Well, I don't even know myself. I just wanted to tell you. I mean, I don't know what I wanted to tell you, but I just wanted you to know about all of this." And then he turned around and went back. So then from what he told me, from what he did, I could really see that something serious was about to happen, that it wasn't some kind of game, and I became more afraid then. Then I went to the lower part of the village to see where everybody was, to see what was happening there. And then at about 12.00, we could hear either the -- we could hear the Hodza saying, "Croats, you have about five minutes to surrender or there will be a massacre something to that effect. So we had this deadline of five minutes. "Croats, you have five minutes to surrender or there will be slaughter." So panic broke out at that time. Everybody was afraid. The civilians were in cellars. Some of them were already in the woods near the stream. A lot of civilians stayed in their homes. We didn't know anything. I was going around trying to meet as many of my people as possible to see what we could do. The majority that I spoke to said, "Well, there's no question of surrender. Did you manage to get in contact with Vitez? What's going on elsewhere?" And I said, "Well, I couldn't reach anybody else in the command. I called about the car and we sent Anto away," and so on. They said, "Well try again." Then I tried to telephone again. I reached the communications centre. I thanked them for the car, and I asked them if they had information whether the ambulance had passed and managed to get to Vitez. They said that they didn't have this information. They would check. They also said that, "We have an ultimatum from the mosque that we have five minutes to surrender, and we have no idea what to do. Is there anything that you could do?" The person that I spoke to from communications, I don't know who was on the phone, things were crazy, we had no time to introduce ourselves, he only said, "Well, UNPROFOR is here right now, and they're going to come to the dividing lines, and then I will convey to the people who are talking there now that they should try to send UNPROFOR there." Then maybe around 12.30, it wasn't that long, we could hear from upper Dubravica that transporters were approaching and there was celebration. We were very happy. And two UNPROFOR APCs arrived at that warehouse that I mentioned. I ran there with another colleague who could speak French a little bit, and I learned a little bit of English in school, so in our bad English and French, we tried, because they were just standing there on the road. So we were behind a bank because we couldn't really come out onto the road because this was from the direction of Jatrenica, Sljivcica, and Vrhovine. It was a clearing, so we were standing on the bank behind some bushes. We were peeking out from there, and we were trying to tell them to move ahead. One of the soldiers had opened the APC door at the top and he looked out, and he was asking us, indicating with his hands, what's going on, and then in English, I spoke English, "Please come here," and for him to go forward about 500 metres, and I hoped to God that they would reach the upper part of the village so that there could be some kind of dividing line established and that shooting could stop, but he just kept on shaking his hand. And then a shell fell some 15 metres away from the APC, and we hid behind the bushes and the bank. They turned the APCs around in the direction of Vitez, and they left. So they never reappeared in the village while we were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that? Did you evacuate civilians then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Well, not yet. That was, perhaps, around 1.00, 2.00. I don't know. We were afraid. I really have no idea. I was running up and down, and I even had two holes in my trousers. Perhaps a bullet had grazed me or something, but in that moment, you couldn't really be aware of the danger involved. Around 2.00 or 2.30, we were pushed away to such an extent, these Croats around their houses, that they came exactly to the dividing line where the last Muslim house was, that is, the middle part of the village, and our line was below that house. That was around 2.00 or 2.30. So we talked then and we said, "There's nothing to wait for anymore. We can try to organise things. What do we do with the women, children, the elderly? And we could also try to withdraw after they had withdrawn." In peaceful times, there were such discussions, what should be done in the case of emergencies, heaven forbid, so either to Mahala or to Krizancevo Selo, those were the two options.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the first place you mentioned? It's called Krtina Mahala?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The place is called Krtina Mahala. We thought that perhaps we could go through that village and forest. There's a creek here, and this is where Krtina Mahala is, approximately; however, on this side (indicating), there was a forest too and a creek that went through Gornja Dubravica, and it went through the forest here to Krizancevo Selo, rather, to Donja Dubravica; however, at that time, none of these roads seemed safe, nor did we believe that we could pull it off. This is Krizancevo Selo (indicating) and then Sljivcica. You could see the forest from down there, but we had to go through Sljivcica, perhaps about 200 metres as the crow flies, so we were aware of the fact that they could hit us with a rifle, a mere rifle, and Sljivcica is over here (indicating). In addition to that, we would have to go on this side towards Vrhovine, and that is where there were far more of them. For about half an hour or so, we were running about, trying to reach an agreement with the civilians too, talking to people who were older, more experienced, wiser, and we sought their advice, and then we finally decided that we would withdraw towards Krizancevo Selo. This was, perhaps, around 3.00, and we agreed that we would go from house to house so that we would be moving from the last Muslim house in the village. So up there, we had no chance to go back because they had already reached -- I mean, the Muslim army had got into the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Croats in the upper part of the village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Well, believe me, at that time, I did not know. I knew in the morning or, rather, around 11.30 when this young man Krehic came back and Abaz too. They said, "Well, you know, there are quite a few military people up there from the outside, and they got quite a few of your people." And then the young man said after that, "Well, they've rallied all the Croats and they've picked them up, and they've taken them to Prnjavor," but I didn't know how many people were actually involved in this. We tried to see whether there were many people staying in houses, and we remembered an elderly woman who lived on her own, and two men went to pick her up. She didn't even manage to get to the shelter on her own. There was one shelter in my house until around 11.00. I have a two-story house. There are these big concrete slabs, and I also had a heating system for central heating, and there was a furnace there. This was a pretty big shelter, about 25 square metres, and about 15 of my neighbours, women and children included, were there. However, later when they started shelling my house more intensely and when the barn was hit and when the windows burst on the house, then we had to evacuate from my house even to the lower part of the village, to other people's places. And then around 3.00 or 3.30 already, we started sending civilians to this creek here (indicating), here (indicating) and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Towards Krizancevo Selo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes, towards Krizancevo Selo. So I was at that house. We were in Brankovic's basement. That's where my family was staying too, my mother, my father, my wife, my two children, my sister-in-law also with two children, and the elderly neighbours, the Jurcevics, the Knezevics, and there is a clearing there about 100 metres, and then you reach the forest. Then about 50 metres away is a creek, and then that creek goes to Krizancevo Selo. At that point, Vlado Ramljak came to see me, and he said, "Dragan, I've come to get you or somebody else too, but they sent me. I was taken prisoner, my wife was taken prisoner, my two sons too, so we are all being held captive in Prnjavor. They sent me to look for some of you guys to come up there to negotiate because the house in Prnjavor is full of our people, and they're asking for your surrender."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is this house in Prnjavor? What is the house you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Oh, the house, the house before the war was called the youth house. That is where dances were held in the evening. For example, in Poculica, it was at the elementary school, and I remember when I was head of the youth organisation in the village, I remember in the evening, we would organise dances there. So in Prnjavor, there was this house called the youth house, and that's where there was a shop on one side, and on this other side, there was this big hall for the young people where they would have dances in the evening. Vlado said to me that they told him that if he didn't come back, they would kill all the rest of his family and that he would have to bring some of us to negotiate, and I said to Vlado, "No problem whatsoever. I'm here, and we'll try to get somebody else. As we move towards the central part of the village where our people are around the houses, we will try to talk to somebody else too and see what the best thing to do would be, but now let us just evacuate the civilians." Actually, these few people who had some kind of weapons, some kind of rifles, we had already sent them off with the civilians so that there wouldn't be an ambush or something. We were quite discouraged. We were frightened. We were afraid that from Sljivcica or Gornja Dubravica they would cut off our road, and this was only about 100 metres away. I mean, the creek was about 100 metres away from the road, so it could easily have been expected for them to come down and to take all these civilians prisoner. The civilians went towards the forest, and Vlado and I went towards the central part of the village along this road that leads to the main road. So he moved onto the main road, but then I thought that I wouldn't take the main road, that I would walk between the houses because my own house was up there too. Our dog was still there, it was still tied up, and also the cattle were there. My wife had left only with a little shopping bag with our children's things because we thought, "Well, come on, we'll be coming back in an hour or two," but what happened happened, and everybody only had their bare necessities, their IDs, their documents. I mean, that is how people left the village, those who managed to leave, that is. I wanted to let my cattle go. The barn had already been hit, but there was a concrete roof so the cattle hadn't been hurt in any way. As we were moving along, there was such a lot of shooting directed at me and Vlado that you couldn't believe it. It was a macadam road. It wasn't an asphalt road. It was terrible. There were bullets flying around us, rocks, stones. Vlado ran towards the main road, and I turned to the left. I stopped by the Jurcevic house, those are my next door neighbours, and then I heard shooting, but the bullets weren't flying around us anymore, and all of this was about 100 metres away from me. The forest was there, and I heard women and children screaming. Then I realised that this somebody who was shooting from Sljivcica was not aiming at Vlado and me any longer, but they had turned their guns towards the civilians because probably he had seen them as they were passing over that clearing I mentioned, and then they started shooting at them in the forest. I tried to run from that house to my own house, this is about 50 metres, and then I thought Vlado would take the right-hand side of the road and I'd take the left-hand side of the road between the houses so nothing would happen. But what happened? I was wounded as I was running that way. I really don't know how come. At first, I had lost consciousness perhaps for 15 or 20 minutes, and I didn't even know how I was wounded, so I'm not sure, but I know that this didn't last long because I managed to catch up with the civilians later on, the ones I had dispatched earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you wounded?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: You mean in terms of my body? I was wounded in the right part of my shoulder blade, and also part of my right ear was torn off, and then also there were some small shrapnel pieces that hit my face and my leg; however, my right shoulder blade was the biggest problem I had. I was even operated on about ten days later and the shrapnel was taken out, and I felt sharp pain there. I was afraid. When I regained consciousness, I simply felt as if I had no legs, as if my legs had been cut off. I tried to crawl to my neighbour's house, they are practically next door, only a few metres away, and then I thought, "Well, if I manage to crawl to his house, I'll crawl to my own house, and perhaps there I will be able to find the simplest way of committing suicide." I simply was not prepared to surrender alive to these Mujahedin, these Muslim forces. Then I started thinking, "What would be the simplest way of killing myself if I didn't have any legs left?" I remembered a boy who had committed suicide earlier on by throwing himself on a hand grenade, and I thought, "Oh, my God, I wish I had a grenade." Then I looked around and I saw that my legs were still there, and I tried to get up, and it was a miracle. I managed to get up and I didn't feel any pain in my legs. So there was blood all over me and I ran down to the forest in the same direction at which the civilians had gone. I found two or three elderly people who were there and they were so excited, one of them was a heart patient, one of them had asthma, so they were sitting there and resting up a bit. When they saw me, they said, "Oh, what happened?" The young men who had already escaped to the forest from their own houses, and they wanted to proceed with the civilians, they bandaged my wounds a bit there and they washed off some of the blood, because I asked them to get the blood off my face, because I knew that I had to hurry. I had to see these civilians, and who could carry me, because this was a forest and it was a difficult terrain, water, rocks, et cetera. It was hard for me to pass by my own children and my mother and my wife, all bloody. So they washed my face a bit, they bandaged my wounds a bit, and I proceeded with another one. So we practically ran in order to catch up with them. We tried to get there as soon as we could, to Krizancevo Selo, so that they could transfer me to a clinic because I was bleeding pretty heavily and I was afraid that I would bleed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When you reached Krizancevo Selo, it was the afternoon, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was the evening, around 5.30 or 6.00. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time did you find out that the Croats, a certain number of Croats were taken prisoner in Poculica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Not at that point. Not yet. Because when I came to Krizancevo Selo, they took me to Vitez in a car to this war clinic. They cleaned my wounds, they bandaged them, they gave me some medicine, and they wanted me to spend the night there. And I asked them, that if there was no special treatment that was to be administered to me, that I would like to go back to Krizancevo Selo. I didn't know where my brother was, where my neighbours were, where my wife and children had ended up. So I said that I would like to go back. And they let me go. They said, "No problem whatsoever." They had given me some shots and they gave me some pills and they said, "If things get worse, try to get someone with a vehicle to bring you back." So then I returned to Krizancevo Selo, and as we were coming in we started to talk and I found my wife and my children in a house there. There was a total of 42 persons there who had sought refuge. Forty-two. So I spent the night sitting in a chair and, you know, people had children sitting in their laps, and my mother and father were there and my uncle and my aunt and my wife, but my aunt and uncle were staying in a house next door. And most of my own folk coming in heard that I was wounded and they wanted to see me. So then I managed to collect some information from them too. I realised that quite a few of our people had remained behind, somebody mentioned 100 people, women, children. However, later on it was realised that in Poculica there were about 70 Croats who remained prisoner. All of them were taken to Prnjavor, some of them to the house, the youth house, and some to the local Muslim houses. Ninety per cent of all the cases it was the Mujahedins who had taken them prisoner. They simply took them prisoner, just like that, and they would take them to a Muslim house and they'd tell the owner of the house, they would say, "Close the downstairs floor and we are going to keep them there." However, we had some very nice examples of some of these local Muslims who were truly embarrassed and they didn't really want their Croat neighbours to be kept prisoner in their houses. So they really treated them nicely. But then also there were some ugly examples of some of the local Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, when were these Croat prisoners set free?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: The Croat prisoners were set free -- well, let me think. I was on sick leave then and I went to see my own folk in Krizancevo Selo, and I think that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they exchanged?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were. And, as far as I can remember, one of the main exchanges took place on the 15th of May, I think, perhaps a month later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all the prisoners exchanged?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: No. After that exchange, about four or five of them remained in the village, elderly people, and also some younger people, a family. They thought that everything would stop within a month's time or so. We had all hoped originally. At the beginning they took them all to the house, the youth house, and finally they let them go and they said they could stay at their houses. So they didn't really want to leave. There were three or four of them, I think. And may I finish, please. A month later they were seeking ways and means of getting to Vitez, and one of them told me that he had given 1.000 Deutschemark to one of these soldiers who were there to take him to the Croat side in Vitez. So after that, after two or three months -- two or three months after the conflict had broken out, not a single Croat had remained in Poculica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they all return alive? That is what I wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Regrettably, no. The first day, after I was wounded, I was told in the evening that Anto Kristo had been killed. He was a man who was born in 1929. So he was the only person who was killed, if one may say so, in some kind of armed conflict. But the rest were taken prisoner and, about a week after they had been taken prisoner, it could have been on the 23rd or 24th of April, perhaps even the 22nd, there was some 20 men and women in this house, in the hall of the youth house, there were about 50 there before, but some were already taken out to dig trenches. And also to bury the cattle that was killed. So at that point there were about 20 of them at the building. And at one point in time they heard clamour in front of the door and also bursts of gunfire. One, two Muslim soldiers shot a burst of gunfire at the door, and in this way at the civilians too. They killed Croats on that occasion who were prisoners. They were my neighbours, Pero Papic, Ivo Vidovic and Jozo Vidovic. And they wounded about six or seven persons. I think two or three were heavily wounded and there were some women too. But they were not local women from Poculica. They were from the village of Putkovici, also a Croat village that the Muslims had taken, and they brought in their prisoners to Prnjavor. When the youth centre in Prnjavor was full, then they sent them to other houses in Preocica and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, the Croat houses in Preocica -- I'm sorry, in Poculica, were they burnt down?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes. I keep talking about the lower and the upper and the central part. The lower part of the village, this Croat part of the village, was totally burned down, all the houses were burned down. In the upper part of the village there were also some houses, and way up towards the border with Vjetrenice, the Tatarevic houses. So a total of 42 Croat houses were burned down in Poculica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the houses that were not burned down?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Well, the ones that were not burned down, that were in this central and upper part of the village, they housed Muslim refugees there, refugees, from Jajce, from Ahmici, Vjetrenica, Travnik, from all over. Now I know that, after the war. At that time I didn't know. But now I know, because these refugees are still staying up there. And I know that recently two or three Croat houses were freed, so-to-speak, that is to say the refugees from Ahmici had left, because their own houses in Ahmici were reconstructed, so they went back there. So these keys moved from hand to hand. They did not return these keys to the Croat owners, but they gave them to a Muslim refugee from the Serb republic who cannot return to there. So, at any rate, all these houses now have a Muslim population -- rather, house Muslim refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's a matter that I want to clarify with the witness. Could you point out on the aerial photograph the village and the upper part and the lower part, so that we can see the bits that you are talking about, please, Mr. Grebenar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. Fine. I am not very familiar with maps, but looking at it from here, this is the settled part, so this part is where there's no -- it's the unpopulated part. And this is the border of Upper Gornja Dubravica and Poculica. Poculica starts from here and then it goes, after this big curve, it goes all the way up to Vjetrenica, along the road. On this curve, the road to Prnjavor forks off and then this is where Poculica borders. So in that part all the houses are mixed, the houses of Croats and Muslims, perhaps the ratio is two Croat homes, two Muslim homes and so on. So this part is mixed. However, this part from here all the way to maybe the centre of the village, this is where the school was. This is where the last Muslim house is. It belongs to Mr. Krehic and Mr. Disdaric, their houses are next to each other. So these are the two houses that I was talking about when I was talking about the village guard. This is where the Muslim guard was and our guard came up to these houses. So this is the central part of the village. And percentage-wise this was 60 to 40 per cent compared to the Croats -- in favour of the Croats. This part here was 100 per cent Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just point, if you would, to the upper part. When you refer to the upper part of the village, where are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What was the bit which was further on, if you follow me further, towards the bend, beyond the bend? Was that part of the village or not? Going the other way. Going this way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean here? Yes. This is the part of the village. There are five or six houses there, because that part of the village is unpopulated, and then there's a kind of secondary road that leads to the cemetery, but along this part of the road all the houses are Croatian. So all of this belonged to the Poculica local community. This is the border of the municipality of Zenica and Vitez. And then this secondary road where it had maybe five, six or 10 Croatian houses, this way there were maybe also 10 to 15 Croatian houses. All the houses were Croatian here. Then along this road, all the homes along this road were Muslim homes, all the way to Vjetrenica. And then in Vjetrenica again these homes here were purely Muslim. And then along, a little bit further along were both Croat and Muslim homes. So this part to the left we had Croatian homes and then to the right of the road were Muslim homes. So the mosque was there. Around the mosque there were both Muslims and Croats. That's where it ends. Then this part here is purely Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. You really helped us a lot in this part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is Gola Kosa here? Can you see it on this aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: I'm not really that good when maps are concerned, but Krtina is here. This is Krtina Mahala. I don't know if that's what you meant. Vrhovine is here. Gola Kosa is east of Vrhovine. So it should be somewhere around here. Well, Nadioci is there, so above Nadioci and above Vrhovine. So it should be somewhere around here. So simply it's kind of more to the right, southeast from Vrhovine and north of Nadioci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I'm right, were there any Croats in Gola Kosa?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes, Gola Kosa -- I'm not 100 per cent sure, but I think it was 100 per cent Croat. There were some houses scattered there. They bordered on Vrhovine. But they were separate. I don't know how many families there were. It wasn't a big village. I think there were three or four families there with their children, with their wives, parents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 16th of April did the Croats from Gola Kosa flee as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes. I know that they fled, but I don't know whether they did it on the 16th or before that. But I know that there are no more Croats in Gola Kosa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Putkovici? You mentioned some captured women from Putkovici who were later accommodated in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Well, I only heard about Putkovici, and I know they are about the Muslim village of Bukve, Sadovace, I heard about that village of Putkovici. I have never been there. I heard about that village from my folk who were captured. I know that there were these women who were brought from Putkovici. So I heard about Putkovici from their reports. I don't know how many families there were. I also know that it was captured by the Muslims and there are no more Croats there. They were expelled then and captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please clarify for the Court where Barin Gaj is, because we will need that. Could you show us that on the aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Well, it should be in this part here. I think that's the part. Krtina is to the left, then there is Pirici, Ahmici, so above Ahmici and Pirici. I think it's this part here. And then there are some small vegetation there. We weren't really that expert. We couldn't really locate where the mortars were, but I think that's where they came from. Then the people who were in the lower part of the village told us that some heavy weapons were being fired from this part here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also indicate where the line of defence was after the conflict of the 16th, the 17th and the 18th, how far in front of your village were they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Well, the line was moved three or four kilometres below our village below Gornja Dubravica, so the line of separation was here. This is the road to Zenica, the Vitez-Zenica road. This is where the road forks off for Sivrino Selo. So the lines of separation were around this road. Our people were below the road and they were above the road. So in the course of the war this would shift 100 metres up or down. And then on one occasion they came as far as 500 metres below, when there was an attack on Krizancevo Selo. That's this part here. So the line went this way up to Krizancevo Selo and then it went around the village to below Tolovici. And then it went on. In the beginning, in peaceful times, our lines were here, up here around Poculica, then above Vrhovine. If this is Barin Gaj. So it is around here. I can't really see. These were all kinds of some points of orientation where we observed, our observation points, observation points for Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the line of defence at that time was established three or four kilometres below the village towards the main road; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to Ahmici, it was in Barin Gaj; is that right? That's where they link up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes. It started from Sivrino Selo, as we said, and then in Krtina Mahala, then Sljivcica was up above there and they would link up here, around Sivrino Selo, and then closer to the road towards Buhine Kuce. This is where Buhine Kuce is. So they were here. This is where the line went. Then it kind of turned back along the outskirts of Krtina Mahala, and then it would link up, go towards Barin Gaj and then up above to Kuber. So that's how the line went, from Barin Gaj to Sljivcica, below Krtina Mahala, this was our line of defence, and then it would drop to Sivrino Selo. And then above Buhine Kuce there was a kind of curve. That's how the line went. Then it came out on the road. Then it went around again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was the closest towards the road?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes. With the expulsion of Croats from Poculica and Gornja Dubravica, they automatically, they automatically gained three or four kilometres of free territory, so they could move the line of defence and link it with Sivrino Selo, Barin Gaj, Tolovici. My arm hurts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the line was established a couple of days after the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, a couple of days, the second or third day. Well, I went to the health clinic for bandaging, but the wounded people would come often and then, from talking with them, I would find out where the lines were located. Throughout the war the line didn't really shift significantly. When the war stopped the line of separation or the checkpoints in '94, when the war stopped, was right here where the road forks off for Sivrino Selo. That's where it remained throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could please look at a very short videotape to see the topography of Tolovici. It's quite interesting because it ties into Ahmici in one part of it and then you could see what the terrain is like.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Grebenar. My house was set on fire a week after we were expelled from here. We can see the accompanying buildings with also a burnt stable, the garage was destroyed. Behind you can see the house of my brother Parica, which was also set on fire and destroyed. Up there further you can see the houses that are not demolished. Opposite is the house of neighbour Ljubo Duvnjak which has also been burnt. All this happened within several days. My house was burnt and then the others were burnt a few days later. This lower part of the village was populated entirely by Croats. Now we can see shots of destroyed and burnt houses of the lower part of the village, and we said before this was entirely populated by Croats. So we are talking about 30 houses which are completely devastated. Also there is one house in the upper part of the village that was destroyed. These are pictures of the house of my next door neighbours, the Jurcevic brothers, and their father whose house was also destroyed. This house had a roof and one can only see the remains. It's been levelled to the ground. This house was also inhabited. It's the house of my next door neighbour. Zdravko Jukovic's house was next door to mine. Now we have a view towards Vrhovine, the neighbouring village, which also belonged to the local community of Poculica, but it was a purely Muslim village, had its separate own name, Vrhovine. It was shelled and fired upon by heavy weapons. Then we can see from this forest somewhere around that that's where the mortars were placed, as far as we could tell. Then we are going down further now towards Barin Gaj, and you can see the hill. That's Barin Gaj. These are the positions where the village was fired upon in the morning of the attack. This is the east view of our village. This is the part towards the upper part of the village where the Croatian houses were untouched and then where Muslims, Bosniaks moved in. We can see here in the background the large hill, it's called Proca Stana. The large Muslim village of Preocica is to the left. This is where the Muslim forces were stationed, or the army, or the Territorial Defence, as it used to be called. So to the north of the village was also a strategic point which was used as a place to fire from. Now we are going to the village of Tolovici towards the northwest. It used to be entirely Serb -- well, not really. It used to be mixed before the war. But the Serbs were expelled by the Muslims, so they left the village before the conflict with the Croats. So this position was also used for the attack on our village. Some heavy weapons, most probably mortars, were located there. This is the view towards Vitez, so Vitez was down towards the south, southwest from us. You can also see the burnt Croatian houses in the village of Gornja Dubravica. You can see the view below my house. This is a stream. There used to be a large forest there, so it was cut down. So it's a kopus (phoen) now. This is where we were evacuating the civilians along the stream withdrawing towards the village of Krizancevo Selo. We were met there by the local population of Gornja Dubravica. That's where we met up below these burnt houses. And then to the right, behind this meadow you can see Krizancevo Selo. This is the view towards Sljivcica. This transmission line up there, it used to be an enemy position, so if you look at it from the forest, this is where they were. And their houses are there down towards the stream, so we were in the forest with the civilians. They opened up the fire from Sljivcica against our civilians. The strongest fire during our retreat came from Sljivcica, because it was the closest point. And you could see as the civilians were evacuating. Now, you can see Barin Gaj again. That's above the village of Ahmici or Gornji Pirici. Up to the left in the forest, there were also mortars and heavy artillery. This is the view towards the village of Vrhovine, and we can see Barin Gaj again, and then from this point, we can see the forest below the village of Krtina Mahala. We can see the houses. I think this is Gornji Pirici above Ahmici. It's a hamlet which joins Ahmici. We have been recording all of this from my house. You can see the bullet holes and shell fragments on the facade of my house, and this is all that is left from the events of that day. There in the background is Sljivcica, and this is the main Vitez-Zenica road via Vjetrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can stop the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Who is this video from?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grebenar, you taped this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes, with a friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: This happened a couple of months ago, maybe three or four months ago. If I can just add, the tape was recorded because there is a committee for the reconstruction and for the return of refugees to the local organisation in Poculica, so we made some documents. The humanitarian organisation taped the villages so that Croats could apply for return, so that's how this cassette, this tape, was made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this tape was made for us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes, and then after that, you asked for something similar, and then I offered the original tape, and you said you weren't interested in something that was so detailed. So based on that previous tape, we made this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you left Poculica and settled at Krizancevo Selo, you went to Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes. I think about a week, I would go to Vitez from Krizancevo Selo to be bandaged and to get my shots, and it was getting crowded in the health centre. There wasn't any room, but I was able to move around, so I had to go and get treatment. I would go from Krizancevo Selo and back. So after a few days in Vitez, I met a friend of mine from work, Jonic, and we're kind of related in a way. My wife and his wife are cousins. So he told me -- he was surprised when he saw me with my bandages. He asked me where I was. "Where's your family? Is everybody alive?" I told him I was in Krizancevo Selo in a house together with my brother's family, with my father, mother. He said, "Well, from Travnik and Grahovcici, there's more and more refugees every day, and I have keys to Sonja's apartment. I think her name was Sonja Covic. She was our colleague who worked in the lab at SPS. And I'm afraid she left me to look after her apartment. She went to her house in Brac." At that time, she was doing some kind of construction, getting her house ready for the summer, for the season, so he offered me the keys to her apartment knowing that I had good relations with Sonja. "I think she would prefer for you to be in that apartment than for some refugee to move in."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you then went to Vitez and also your brother and his family?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Our whole family, my brother's family, my family, my mother and father, came to that two-room apartment that belonged to Sonja.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can take a break, and then we have another brief video recording and maybe a few questions. So maybe this is a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, let us now have a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number of the videotape was D59/2. The English translation is D59A/2, and the BCS version is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The BCS translation D59B/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn now for thirty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grebenar, we're going to look at the other tape now. It's comprised of several parts, so you can tell us what each part is about. The events that are depicted is the shelling of Vitez in June of '93, but in view of the fact that a lot of the witnesses are going to talk about this event or they've mentioned this event, including Witness DA/5 regarding the case of Hakija Chengic, so if you can tell us what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Here is the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number of the videotape is D60/2, the English translation, D60A/2, and the BCS translation, D60B/2. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grebenar, there is no translation for this part. Could you tell us who these children are?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes. You can see me here bandaged, and the first little boy is my brother's son. This is my daughter and then my brother's daughter, and then on the left, the smallest child is my son. This is my brother's son who was 12 at the time. This was filmed three or four days after we had arrived in Krizancevo Selo when we were refugees. This is my daughter who was 9 then, just like my brother's daughter who is sitting next to her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was your brother's daughter?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: She was also 9 at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your brother's son?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: He was 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was filmed in Krizancevo Selo when you went there as refugees?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He escaped together with you; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: At that time, he was 66 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we proceed, please? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what can we see in this section of the film?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: This shows the evening of the 10th of June when a Muslim shell fell on the children's playground. You can see a bench here that they had made for themselves. This was in town, in Vitez, in a suburb, actually, right by the high school. A shell fell, and on that occasion, it killed eight children. Five of them died on the spot. Among these children were the two children of my brother's whom you had seen, and the boy is my brother's son whom we saw a few minutes ago in the picture. My father brought him here, and you can see my father in the background collecting the bits and pieces of glass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The little girl we saw on that video, she was also killed too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the late Tina, yes, and she was still showing signs of life. My brother went to the hospital together with her, but she died during surgery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is this that we see now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: That morning when we were burying the five children who were killed on the spot, I was there on my own with the late Velimir. My brother had gone to the hospital. I don't know what had happened to the little Tina. These are the parents of the children who were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is no one attending the funeral, the mothers, no one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Well, this was taking place early in the morning. We always conducted our funerals very early in the morning or very late at night because they would open fire on the cemetery and the people who were involved, so it was a risky business. You see, we are burying five children, and there are not more than seven or eight of us altogether, including the young men who were digging the graves. These are Dragan Ramljak's parents, and I was here and the late Velimir. At this moment, my brother-in-law came and said that Tina also died during surgery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's 6.00 in the morning, right, we can see it on the film?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could we have the volume up a bit? This is one of the wounded children. Well, we can't really hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We were sitting at the table talking and laughing. And what happened then? All of a sudden, the shell hit the ground and I heard only the sound, and then I saw people running and crying. Where were you wounded? My legs and head were wounded. How do you feel now? Better. Do you know who was wounded or killed? Yes, I do. From the very most moment when it happened, I saw everything and I knew everything, and I was conscious all the time. What do you think about all of that? I don't know. Thank you. Good luck and get better as soon as possible. How old are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have finished now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, this boy who was on this last piece of footage, what's his name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: His name is Ivan Garic and his house is there. He was not a refugee. He lived where my brother and my mother and my father and my brother's late children were staying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his brother and sister, were they killed too?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. This boy's brother and sister were killed, so these were two families, Mr. Mile Garic's two children were killed and my brother's two children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was a terrible shock, this event, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Well, what else could have it been? It was terrible and incredible. It took us a long time to find our peace. We will never find our peace with that. I keep saying, until the present day, that this was premeditated, that is to say that somebody actually aimed at this, fully conscious of what he was doing, inflicting such evil, because the defence line of the HVO was about 1.000 metres away from that place. That is where the closest point was. There weren't any strategic facilities there, nothing was nearby, headquarters or whatever. This was a settlement, this was between houses, it was a peaceful area. That is the only playground that the children had. They didn't want to go anywhere else because they thought it was much more dangerous to go anywhere else because this was surrounded by houses on all sides. This was about 100 square metres of clear ground where they had enough space, and their parents and they themselves thought they were the safest there. They didn't even let them go out there very often either. If the town was being shelled or something, of course they stayed indoors. But that day was peaceful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did any of the Croats return to Poculica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: No. No. None of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Croat houses, were they reconstructed? We can see in this picture, in this film that they were not.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: No, not a single Croat house in Poculica has been renewed as yet. I mentioned some time ago that we are carrying out preparations for this, and we have registered with various humanitarian organisations, international organisations. We are trying to get our turn to have our houses reconstructed. But, to tell you the truth, the situation is such, I think, that it is not really favourable for returning, because we have our own cemetery there and during the war the Muslim army totally devastated the cemetery, the fence, the tombstones. The tombstones were devastated in 60 per cent of all cases, the crosses, everything. The small chapel that is at the cemetery, it was burned down too. And after the war when the right conditions were created, I think it was in '97 or so, in '97, in agreement with the Muslim side, through the municipality, the IPTF, the SFOR, we organised the repair of the chapel at the cemetery and the reconstruction of the fence. We could not have built at that point the beautiful kind of concrete fence that existed before, but at least we put a wire fence around it because we didn't want the cattle, at least, to go into the cemetery and graze, as they had been doing until then. So we did that with the assistance of the police, the international police, the IPTF, the SFOR, and there were no incidents. We did this during the course of a single day. We, the villagers of Poculica had organised ourselves and we made an announcement to them and everything was done within one day, as I said. The chapel was reconstructed, painted, and then also the crosses that were knocked over were put up again, and then the grass was taken care of, so it is almost normal looking now. However, unfortunately, this did not last long. We have a video recording of that too, when we did all of that during that one day, the fence and everything else, but a few months later the same thing happened again, they knocked over all the crosses. In addition to the ones that had been knocked over before, they broke a few other ones too. We went there and repaired it once again. Now, in '98, again they burnt down our chapel for the third time. They took away this fence, this wire that we put around the cemetery, and they broke about seven to 10 tombstones. The IPTF was informed of this and the local police and everybody, but nobody ever did a thing. As the inhabitants of Poculica, we are very disappointed by this, and this makes the possibility of our return unsafe too. However, if our houses are reconstructed, we'll go back, but we are not pleased with this, three or four years after the war such things are still happening and the local police, which is a joint one, a joint Muslim-Croat police force now, they do not find it in their interest, nor does the IPTF, to find the perpetrators of all of this devastation. There are also some local Muslims who said they practically know the names of the people who did this, and that it is people from other parts who do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grebenar, we also saw the mosque with the minaret in this video footage. Which village did this mosque belong to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: We actually saw two, if you are referring to the video cassette that we saw before. Yes. One is in the village of Vrhovine and that is where they had their own mezar, their own cemetery. I am not very knowledgeable as far as their religious places are concerned, but there wasn't a mosque there. They only had a cemetery. Also we saw the mosque in Poculica. The mosque has been there forever, but now it was reconstructed, practically, with these joint funds. The Muslims invested more, truth to tell, but it was not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was not damaged during the war, was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards Poculica, one more question. Please tell the Court, what is the amount of weapons that the Croats had on the 16th of April, 1993 when the attack came?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Well, we think, I think, this Crisis Staff of ours thought that we had about 30 odd rifles, some hunting guns and others -- well, about 30 altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a rifle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did. I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry. Just one more thing. I would like to have Defence Exhibit 41/2 shown to the witness. Please read Section 5 of this report.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: "From the direction of Vjetrenica and Vrhovine the Muslim forces are shooting at Croat houses. The locals are calling and panic-stricken, asking what they should do, because their houses do not have any basements."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is a combat report of the Vitez Brigade dated the 16th of April, 1993 at 9.00, and the part that you read just now corresponds to the situation in Poculica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Precisely. I didn't know at the time, but quite a few of us had the numbers of the Crisis Staff in Vitez. It wasn't that I was only in contact with them, but other people were frightened and they sought advice and help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also the fact that they were shooting from the direction of Vjetrenica and Vrhovine. That is correct too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I call this a frontal attack. And it was taking place from there, from Vjetrenica and Vrhovine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement you also mentioned that on the 15th of April, 1993 you saw Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Vitez. And he was together with Senad Topoljak?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how well did you know Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Zoran Kupreskic, we were on very good terms. How should I put it? We were the best of friends. We visited each others homes, we also knew each other at work. All of it started in 1983, when we started working together in the factory, and then after about a year, when we were stationed at the same facility and where we shared the same entrance, the same hallway, our offices were nearby. And we practically spent about eight hours together every day at work, together with Mr. Topoljak, and the others who were there, Franjo Rajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Senad Topolac, is he a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: He is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else were you on friendly terms with from work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Well, at work we were friends with Franjo Rajic, a Croat. I should mention who is who, right? And Nisret Ramic, a Muslim; Ahmet Mahmutovic, a Muslim; Zijad Tarahija, a Muslim; Zoran Kupreskic, a Croat too; Dragan Grebenar, that's me, I am also a Croat; Hrustic Sead, a Muslim, and so on. This was a group. And we were closely linked together due to our work and also we became friends at home, apart from work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During 1992 and 1993 very important things took place. Politics prevailed in all spheres of life. Tell me, what were the positions of Zoran Kupreskic that he presented during your conversations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic's positions in relation to all of this were sometimes beyond my own understanding, because, as you said, politics prevailed everywhere, and politics determined everything. The war had already broken out in Croatia and I already mentioned that we were friends, all of us there, the Croats and everything. But we all had our own angle, so-to-speak. For example, I condemned the Serb aggression, whereas Mahmutovic, for example, and Topoljak, a bit more moderately would try to find some justification, and say, "Well, the Croats are to be blamed too." And I was irritated in all these conversations, because Mr. Zoran Kupreskic behaved either by silently agreeing with Senad Topoljak and sometimes voicing his agreement with him. Sometimes, because of these views of his, sometimes he and I differed in our views and we had debated these points a bit. He was apolitical. He did not look at things politically. He tried to listen to both sides. He didn't point his finger at anyone. Perhaps I am a bit different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear him express some extremist nationalist views in any situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: No way. Not him. I must tell the Court about this, but all people who knew Zoran -- I mean, such questions and even such claims sound ridiculous to people who know Zoran. The locals of Vitez and the villagers from his part know that he was very popular among the Muslims and the Serbs there. He had so many friends there. He really put his work and his family first, and also this folklore, this music, this cultural society where he was. Then quite a few young people were there, and they simply did not talk about different ethnicity or whatever. Not very many people in Vitez did at that time. But he was the one who preserved the cultural society. After the elections when Napredek, a Croatian cultural society, was supposed to be established, he initiated the idea because -- well, naturally, the Muslims who belonged to this cultural society before, I can't remember the name, I think it was also called Slobodan Princip Seljo before. And he found it kind of embarrassing that it would be called a Croatian cultural society. He felt this before they did. He even insisted with our own people who wanted to set up that kind of a cultural society that they should remain together under a different name. And I think that he actually succeeded in this effort. And I think it was called the municipal cultural society of Vitez, where they continued to play instruments, sing and dance together. Muslims, Croats and Serbs. So, truth to tell, in those times Zoran, perhaps, had Croats viewing him unkindly rather than Muslims, because practically he did not work in the interest of the Croats as much as he did in the interest of all others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that he would take food to Gacice in 1993 to one of his co-workers from work, to some of his co-workers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN GREBENAR (Cont'd)
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that because I saw him in front of the building when the crime in Ahmici happened. Zoran came to Vitez and he never returned to this place, Ahmici. And we even lived in the same building. And I saw him with another co-worker, another Croat, and they were loading oil, flour, something into a car. And I asked him, "Where are you going?" And I thought that he was going somewhere, taking this. Then he said, "We are taking this to Sead Hrustic." He had seen him in Vitez before and Hrustic had asked him whether -- I don't know. He ran out of oil and flour and Hrustic -- told him that he ran out of oil and flour and that he needed it. And then Zoran Kupreskic, together with this other co-worker, loaded this into his car and they took it to Hrustic. I'm sure that this gentleman can confirm this, although I didn't go with them.
